questions.question: The linear momentum of a particle is the product of its mass and which other quantity?
questions.explanation: Linear momentum is defined as p = mv, the product of mass and velocity. Acceleration, displacement, and force do not define momentum.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the direction of the momentum vector of a moving particle?
options: It is always directed vertically downward
It is opposite to the particle's velocity
It is the same as the particle's velocity
It is perpendicular to the particle's velocity
questions.explanation: Since p = mv and mass is a positive scalar, the momentum vector points in the same direction as the velocity.

questions.question: The SI unit of linear momentum is expressed as
questions.explanation: From p = mv, the unit is kg m s−1, which equals N s (since 1 N = 1 kg m s−2). J s is angular momentum, kg m s−2 is force, and W is power.

questions.question: Impulse is the product of force and which quantity?
questions.explanation: Impulse is J = FΔt, the product of force and the time over which it acts. Force × distance gives work.

questions.question: The impulse–momentum theorem states that the impulse delivered to an object is equal to its
questions.explanation: The impulse–momentum theorem states J = Δp: impulse equals the change in momentum. Change in kinetic energy relates to work, not impulse.

questions.question: A system is described as isolated when
options: No particles enter or leave the system
The net external force acting on it is zero
The total kinetic energy of the system remains constant
The internal forces between particles vanish
questions.explanation: An isolated system is one on which the net external force is zero, so its total momentum is conserved. No particles entering/leaving (A) describes a closed system.

questions.question: The law of conservation of linear momentum applies to a system that is
questions.explanation: Conservation of linear momentum requires both that the system be closed (no mass exchange) and isolated (no net external force).

questions.question: The law of conservation of momentum follows directly from
questions.explanation: Internal forces come in equal and opposite action-reaction pairs by Newton's third law, so they cancel and the total momentum stays constant.

questions.question: In an elastic collision, which two quantities are both conserved?
options: Kinetic energy and total energy only
questions.explanation: An elastic collision conserves both total momentum and total kinetic energy.

questions.question: A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved is described as
questions.explanation: An inelastic collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy — some kinetic energy is converted into other forms such as heat or deformation.

questions.question: In a completely inelastic collision, the colliding bodies
options: Bounce apart without any energy loss
Stick together and move as one
Separate with the same relative speed
questions.explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and move with a common final velocity; this is the case of maximum kinetic energy loss.

questions.question: For a perfectly elastic collision, what is the value of the coefficient of restitution?
questions.explanation: A perfectly elastic collision has e = 1, because the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach.

questions.question: A coefficient of restitution of zero corresponds to which type of collision?
options: A collision in which the bodies bounce apart
A collision that releases additional energy
questions.explanation: When e = 0, the relative speed of separation is zero, so the bodies move together after impact — a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.question: A bullet embedding itself in a stationary block is an example of
options: A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved
A collision that generates extra kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Since the bullet and the block move together afterwards, this is a perfectly inelastic collision. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

questions.question: Which pair of quantities are both vectors?
questions.explanation: Impulse (force × time) and momentum both have magnitude and direction, so both are vectors. Mass and kinetic energy are scalars.

questions.question: A moving ball strikes a wall and rebounds. The impulse on the ball is directed
questions.explanation: The ball's momentum reverses, so the change in momentum (impulse) is directed away from the wall, in the direction of the rebound.

questions.question: The change in momentum of an object is equal to
options: The net force acting on it
questions.explanation: By the impulse–momentum theorem, Δp = J — the change in momentum equals the impulse applied to the object.

questions.question: Which statement about an inelastic collision is correct?
options: Kinetic energy is conserved although momentum is not conserved
Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
questions.explanation: In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not (some is converted to heat, sound, and deformation).

questions.question: In a perfectly elastic head-on collision between two identical masses where one is at rest, the incident mass
options: Comes to rest after the impact
Continues with half its original speed
questions.explanation: For equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision with one at rest, the masses exchange velocities, so the incident mass comes to rest after impact.

questions.question: The impulse of a force acting on a body is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: Impulse = force × time, so the SI unit is the newton-second (N s). Joules and newton-metres are units of energy or work.

questions.question: A closed system is one in which
options: The net external force is zero
No particles enter or leave the system
The total kinetic energy of the system remains constant
questions.explanation: A closed system exchanges no mass with its surroundings, so no particles enter or leave. Isolation (zero net external force) is a separate condition.

questions.question: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two moving bodies, the final kinetic energy is
options: Always greater than the initial value
Always equal to the initial value
Always less than the initial value
Sometimes equal to the initial value
questions.explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and the maximum possible kinetic energy is lost, so the final kinetic energy is always less than the initial value.
